content.promptText:
Shot type: Tight chest-up corporate headshot, camera at eye level, portrait orientation — the standard crop for a LinkedIn/executive-bio headshot (top of head to mid-chest, with headroom above).

Subject: Using the uploaded photo as the exact identity reference, a photorealistic corporate headshot of the sitter — bone structure, eye shape, nose, jawline, and skin texture locked to the reference, zero reshaping, zero beautification, unmistakably the same person, natural skin with visible pores and fine texture retained. Only wardrobe, lighting, and set change. Pose: shoulders angled ~20° off camera, chin lifted a touch to lengthen the neck, weight on the back foot, a relaxed closed-mouth or slight genuine smile, eyes reading confident and warm, not performative. Wardrobe: [WARDROBE, e.g. a tailored charcoal blazer over a crisp white shirt] — pressed, collar sitting flat, no distracting pattern moiré.

Environment/Setting: a seamless medium-grey (roughly 18% grey) paper studio backdrop, lit two stops under key so it reads as a soft gradient rather than a flat card — the kind of set a top LinkedIn/annual-report photographer would light.

Lighting: key is a 36in (90cm) octabox at camera-left, 45° off axis and 15° above eye line, feathered slightly away from the face to avoid hot spots, producing soft falloff with a small controlled shadow under the far cheek. Fill is a 4x6ft white bounce card camera-right at roughly -1.7 stops relative to key, opening the shadow side without flattening it. A small grid spot or strip-box adds hair/rim light from slightly behind the subject at low power, lifting the hairline and shoulder edge off the backdrop. Overall ratio lands around 3:1, with clean round catchlights at 10-11 o'clock in both eyes.

Camera/Lens: an elevated eye-level portrait shot as if on a full-frame body with an 85mm lens at f/2 — the classic portrait focal length, whose compression flatters facial proportions without the nose-forward distortion a 35-50mm would introduce at this distance — a touch of focus margin across both eyes while the background falls into a soft creamy wash. Focus locked on the near eye's iris; eyelashes crisp, skin texture real, not frequency-separated to plastic.

Style/Mood: true-to-life, slightly warm skin tones, gentle contrast, no crushed blacks, no HDR halos — confident, polished, corporate-editorial.

Avoid / negative prompt: waxy or plastic skin, blown highlights on the forehead or nose, mismatched catchlight direction, harsh on-camera flash, distorted or reshaped features, extra or fused fingers, heavy makeup-filter look, text or watermarks.

Parameters: vertical portrait orientation, 4:5 aspect ratio, ultra-detailed, high resolution.
- Midjourney: --ar 4:5 --style raw --v 6.1 --no plastic skin, warped hands, extra fingers, watermark (--style raw suppresses the model's default beautification bias so the real-skin-texture instruction actually holds).
- Gemini (Nano Banana): state the ratio in plain language within the prompt text ("aspect ratio 4:5") — read directly, no flag required. Keep the Shot type → Subject → Environment → Lighting → Camera → Lens ordering above, which is the template Imagen-family models parse most reliably.
- gpt-image / DALL·E: no exact 4:5 size is exposed; request size 1024x1536 (closest supported portrait ratio) and crop to 4:5 afterward if the exact ratio matters.

Consistency note: this is an image-edit/reference prompt (attach your photo) rather than a from-scratch generation. Midjourney's --cref/--cw and Gemini's Nano Banana image-editing mode hold a face reliably within one edit; OpenAI's gpt-image/DALL·E is documented by OpenAI as weaker at keeping an exact face consistent across repeated, separate generations, so expect more drift there if you regenerate several variations — regenerate and pick the best match rather than expecting perfect repeatability.

whatYouGet: A decisive-moment lifestyle scene — product mid-action (mid-pour, mid-grip, mid-lift), not a static pose — shot from the person's shoulders down so the focus stays on the product and the action
Single-source window-light realism (3200-4000K raking key, no fill card) with true 35mm f/2.0-f/2.8 depth-of-field separation between the tack-sharp product and a softly blurred setting
Genuine environmental wear (a water ring, a linen crease) instead of stock-photo staging, with a clean low-detail zone reserved for overlay text, at 4:5
content.promptText:
Resolution/Format: High-resolution editorial lifestyle photograph, shot as though on a full-frame mirrorless body (36-45MP) for genuine texture resolution, portrait orientation, aspect ratio 4:5 (Midjourney: --ar 4:5; Nano Banana/Gemini: state "aspect ratio 4:5, portrait orientation" in plain language in the sentence — it reads the ratio directly, no flag required).

Product: [PRODUCT] captured at the decisive moment (the instant a gesture, light and composition align) — a model's hands, or a person framed from the shoulders down with face out of frame or three-quarters turned away, [ACTION, e.g. holding it, pouring from it, opening the lid] caught mid-gesture: fingers mid-grip with real pressure-blanching at the knuckle, liquid mid-pour with a visible arc and a few airborne droplets (implying a fast sync shutter, ~1/500s, freezing motion without blur), a lid mid-lift with real hinge-torque body language. Product placed on the lower or right third per the rule of thirds, with the implied gesture's motion line pointing back into the frame rather than out of it.

Surface/Background: Set in [REAL SETTING, e.g. a sunlit kitchen counter, a cafe table, a home desk], blocked the way an editorial food-and-product photographer stages a scene — not a studio sweep. Genuine, specific surface wear (a water ring with a faint hard edge where it's dried, a soft diagonal crease in linen, a hairline chip in a mug's glaze catching a highlight) placed only where a real environment would actually produce it, never as decorative clutter; slight, natural asymmetry in every prop's placement and rotation, resisting any stock-photo symmetry or perfectly parallel edges. Reserve one clean, low-detail passage of background (roughly a third of the frame, one consistent tonal value, no strong texture) as an overlay-text-safe zone — check it reads under both a white and a dark headline before finalizing.

Lighting: A single large source acting as key — natural window light, raking in from camera-left at a low afternoon angle (roughly 20-30° above the subject, 3-4 stops brighter than ambient) so it skims across the product's surface at a grazing incidence that reveals real texture (label emboss, condensation beading, brushed-metal grain) rather than flattening it under a frontal fill. No fill card or bounce — the far side of the product falls into a soft, physically accurate falloff (inverse-square, not a hard-edged studio shadow) the way a single window actually behaves. Color temperature warm and singular (~3200-4000K), locked and consistent across product, skin and surface — no mixed daylight/tungsten color casts, no green cast from unseen fluorescent fill.

Camera/Angle: As though shot on a 35mm-equivalent prime at f/2.0-f/2.8 on a full-frame sensor, focus locked precisely on the product's single nearest sharp edge (a label's leading letterform, a cap's rim, a woven-texture crest) so it reads as the unmistakable tack-sharp anchor, while [REAL SETTING] falls into a soft, creamy two-to-three-plane bokeh behind it — enough optical separation that the product visually detaches from its background without a cut-out look.

Focus/Material detail: Palette: [PALETTE, e.g. warm neutrals of wood, linen and pale light], color-graded so skin tones stay physiologically correct (no orange/waxy skew from the warm key) and the product's true label/packaging color isn't shifted by the warm cast — verify against the product's real Pantone/hex if known. Avoid: obvious stock-photo staging, waxy or plastic-rendered skin, extra, fused or distorted fingers (a documented failure mode at close hand crops), competing third-party logos, on-camera flash, harsh unflattering top-down shadows, added text, watermarks.

Platform note: tuned for Midjourney (append --ar 4:5, optionally --style raw to keep the window-light grade literal rather than MJ's default punch) and Google Nano Banana/Gemini (paste as continuous prose — the "aspect ratio 4:5" and lighting-direction language is parsed directly, no flags). content.promptText:
Resolution/Format: High-resolution top-down editorial flat-lay photograph, shot as though from a copy-stand or overhead boom arm (not handheld — parallax error is the giveaway of a handheld "top-down" shot), square format, aspect ratio 1:1 (Midjourney: --ar 1:1; OpenAI gpt-image/DALL·E: state "top-down flat lay, square 1:1 crop" plainly in the opening sentence).

Product: [PRODUCT] as the hero, styled with [COMPLEMENTARY PROPS, e.g. fresh herbs, a folded linen cloth, a ceramic mug, scattered ingredients] using a stylist's rule-of-odds arrangement (odd numbers of grouped objects read as more natural and less "arranged" than even pairs): props grouped in threes or fives at varying scale, rotation and z-height (some flat, one slightly propped for a shadow break) so the eye enters at the product and travels through the frame on a loose diagonal, with one quadrant left deliberately empty rather than symmetrically balanced — asymmetric balance (large object near-frame, small cluster far-frame) rather than mirror symmetry.

Surface/Background: [SURFACE, e.g. warm beige textured plaster, pale oak, handmade paper] — texture visible at macro scale but never competing with the product's own surface detail. A disciplined three-to-four-color story built on a 60-30-10 distribution around [PALETTE, e.g. warm terracotta, cream and sage] — dominant surface tone at 60%, prop palette at 30%, one accent color at 10% — props and surface chosen to sit within that palette rather than color-corrected after the fact. Reserve one genuinely empty, low-texture zone [upper right / center] at consistent tone and even lighting — sized and positioned like a real logo/caption slot, not leftover negative space.

Lighting: Camera on a copy-stand or overhead boom, sensor plane dead-parallel to the surface — zero keystoning, meaning a square prop reads perfectly square in frame with no perspective convergence at any edge. A single soft, broad source (large octabox, 4x4 diffusion scrim, or equivalent open shade) directly overhead and offset slightly camera-left, so every shadow in the frame falls in the same direction at the same shallow length — the single visual tell that separates "one real light source" from an AI-generated flat lay with conflicting shadow directions. No fill needed at this softness; specular highlights on any glossy prop (ceramic glaze, glass) stay soft-edged, never a hard clipped hotspot.

Camera/Angle: As though on a 50mm (or 100mm macro for tighter product crops) at f/8-f/11 on a full-frame sensor — enough depth of field, combined with the flat overhead plane, that the entire frame resolves evenly sharp corner to corner (there's no depth axis to selectively defocus in a true top-down, so any edge softness reads as a lens or focus error, not style).

Focus/Material detail: Every micro-texture (herb veining, cloth weave, ceramic glaze crackle) rendered crisply; the product label stays perspective-true (a genuinely parallel camera needs zero keystone correction) and fully legible. Note: exact, readable label copy is a documented weak point across current image models — most acutely on gpt-image/DALL·E — so treat any close-crop label text as a first draft; verify at full resolution and expect to regenerate the crop or clean the type in an editor. Grade clean and editorial, moderate saturation, never oversaturated. Avoid: clutter, competing brand logos, any camera tilt or converging lines, muddy mixed-direction shadows, uneven light falloff across the frame, added text, watermarks.

name: Minimal Vector Logo Mark
summary: A clean, geometric symbol mark that stays instantly recognizable from a favicon to a billboard.
description: A clean, geometric symbol mark that stays instantly recognizable from a favicon to a billboard.

whatYouGet: A logomark built in Subject → Construction geometry → Color/style → Background/negative-space → Aspect-ratio order: the symbol concept engineered on a golden-ratio modular grid rather than drawn freehand

A symmetry/asymmetry choice deliberately tied to the brand's core value (stability vs. momentum), a single flat fill or one constant stroke weight, and negative space carrying a genuine secondary meaning (the FedEx-arrow method)

A silhouette pressure-tested at both extremes — legible at a 16px favicon and intentional-looking at billboard scale — in a color chosen to still hold contrast in black-only or single-color reproduction
content.promptText:
Subject: a minimalist vector logomark for [BRAND NAME], a company that [WHAT THE BRAND DOES]. Core concept: [SYMBOL IDEA, e.g. an abstract mountain merged with an upward arrow] — a single isolated symbol mark, no scene, no supporting elements, no ground plane. Let the brand's core value dictate the composition, the way real identity systems are briefed: bilateral symmetry on a vertical axis if the value is stability, trust or permanence (banks, insurers, legacy institutions lean this way); a single rotated, truncated or off-axis element breaking symmetry if the value is momentum, speed or innovation, so the eye reads directional motion rather than static balance.

Construction geometry: build it the way a senior identity designer actually constructs a mark — from an underlying grid of circles, half-circles, tangent arcs and 45°/90° angle guides, scaled in a golden-ratio (1:1.618, Fibonacci-adjacent) progression the way marks like the Twitter bird, Pepsi globe and Apple logo are documented as gridded, snapping every anchor point and tangent to that grid so the mark reads as engineered rather than freehand-drawn. Render in exactly one of two disciplined systems: a solid flat fill with zero interior linework and no internal cutouts beyond the core negative-space device, or a single uniform stroke weight held mathematically constant through every curve, corner and terminal and never tapered — pick whichever preserves the silhouette better at a 16px crush. Hold optical balance rather than mathematical center: a heavier or larger sub-shape sits fractionally lower and further left than pure geometry dictates, correcting for the eye's tendency to read top-heavy mass as visually unstable (the same correction type designers apply to round letterforms overshooting the baseline).

Color and style: a single flat [COLOR] value, chosen with enough luminance contrast against pure white (sanity-checked the way an accessibility contrast ratio would be, even outside a text context) that the mark still reads unambiguously when converted straight to true grayscale or pure black — it will inevitably be reproduced in foil stamp, laser engraving, single-spot-color print or embroidery, none of which forgive a mark that only works in color.

Background and negative space: an isolated mark on a plain white background, clear-space equal to roughly half the mark's own height held on all four sides (the standard logo clear-space convention). Use the negative space inside and around the form as a genuine second signal, not decoration — overlap or subtract shapes so a secondary, legible form emerges only on a second look, the way the FedEx wordmark hides an arrow in the Ex, or the WWF panda is built from four solid black shapes with the white page doing the rest. Pressure-test the composition at both size extremes: it must remain one clean, unclogged shape at a 16px browser-tab favicon, and it must still read as deliberately engineered rather than merely simplistic blown up to billboard scale.

Aspect ratio and format: square, delivered perfectly vector-clean, no raster artifacts, no anti-aliasing halo. --ar 1:1 --v 6.1 --style raw --no wordmark, tagline, letters, drop shadow, bevel, 3D render, gradient, photorealism, any micro-detail finer than would survive a 2mm embroidery patch.

Platform note: built for Midjourney and Ideogram, both of which hold clean flat-vector geometry more reliably than photoreal-leaning models; there's no lettering in this mark so text-rendering limitations don't apply. For genuinely editable output, redraw the accepted result in Illustrator or Figma using the same grid logic described above rather than tracing it as-is.

content.promptText:
Subject: a premium app icon for [APP NAME], an app that [WHAT IT DOES], centered on a single bold glyph representing [CORE FUNCTION] reduced to its most essential silhouette — one shape, one idea, no secondary element, no background scene — to the standard a senior product-design team ships to the App Store and Google Play review queues.

Construction geometry: construct the tile as a true superellipse (squircle, superellipse exponent ≈5, per Apple's published Human Interface Guidelines corner formula — not a simple rounded-rectangle, which is mathematically flatter through the corner and is exactly why generic icons look subtly "off" next to native ones). Hold the glyph to a consistent optical size relative to the tile, roughly 55-65% of the tile's visual field measured by its bounding shape (not its literal bounding box — round or diagonal glyphs need to sit slightly larger than square ones to read as equal size, the same optical-correction principle type designers use), with even breathing room on all sides, never touching or bleeding past the superellipse edge. Anti-alias every edge to sub-pixel precision — no jagged raster edges at any zoom level.

Color and style: a smooth diagonal gradient from [COLOR] at the top-left to [SECOND COLOR] at the bottom-right, using analogous hues 30-60° apart on the color wheel (not complementary) so it reads as premium and cohesive rather than a garish two-tone clash — this is roughly the hue-distance range used by most top App Store icons in the productivity and finance categories. Add exactly two restrained depth cues and no more: a soft inner shadow along the top edge for a subtly recessed feel, and a faint 1-2% opacity highlight along the bottom-right consistent with the gradient's implied upper-left light source — matte and modern throughout, never glossy, wet or bevelled in the 2009 skeuomorphic style. Render the glyph in crisp white or the single highest-contrast tone available against the tile, checked to hold a strong, legible silhouette when desaturated to pure grayscale (accessibility and low-power display modes render icons this way on some platforms).

Background and negative space: the gradient tile is the entire background — no separate backdrop, mockup frame, drop shadow outside the tile, or device bezel — with the glyph's breathing room doing all the negative-space work. Mentally verify legibility at 40px (home-screen size) and 29px (Settings-row size), not only at full 1024px export resolution — icons live almost entirely at these small sizes.

Aspect ratio and format: square, delivered at 1024×1024 (the source size both stores require before their own auto-scaling to every device size). --ar 1:1 --no text, letters, numbers, busy secondary detail, photorealism, outer border, stroke, watermark, drop shadow outside the tile, gradient banding.

Platform note: renders cleanly in both Midjourney and Google Nano Banana/Gemini, which both handle gradient tiles, true superellipse geometry and soft directional shading well; there's no text in this icon so no legibility pass is needed on the glyph itself. Run the accepted 1024px result through an icon-set generator afterward to produce every required export size (20pt-1024pt) — this prompt only produces the master tile.

content.promptText:
Subject: a set of 6 minimalist line icons representing [LIST CONCEPTS, e.g. speed, security, support, growth, automation, insight], built to the discipline of a real production icon-system spec — the same rigor as Feather Icons, Material Symbols or Phosphor — not six unrelated sketches that merely share a stroke color.

Hold one stroke weight, 2px at this 24px scale, constant across all six icons, with rounded caps and rounded joins applied consistently — never mix round and butt/miter terminals within one set, since mismatched line-endings is the single fastest tell that an icon set was assembled from different sources rather than designed as one family.

Color and style: a single flat [COLOR] stroke with no fill anywhere in the set, resisting any decorative flourish, drop shadow or secondary weight — restraint at this stroke weight is what makes an icon system read as professional infrastructure rather than illustrative decoration.

Background and negative space: all six icons arranged in one evenly gauged horizontal row on a clean white background, separated by identical gutter spacing roughly equal to one icon-width, with no containers, keylines, circles or background shapes behind any glyph. Every icon should be instantly parseable as its concept in under a second at actual UI rendering size (16-24px) — that half-second read, not how it looks blown up on a slide, is the real test of a working line icon.

A single grazing-incidence key light (warm ~3000–4500K) that rakes long shadows across the terrain for real scale, with volumetric fog acting as natural fill and scattering it into visible god-rays

content.promptText:
A photorealistic, low-angle wide-angle cinematic establishing shot, framed the way a film's opening shot is blocked — camera positioned at knee-height rather than an aerial drone survey, so the horizon sits low in frame and the scene reads as monumental rather than merely surveyed from above. The shot opens on [SCENE, e.g. a lone timber cabin on a misty mountainside], placed off-center per the rule of thirds, with a strong foreground anchor (a boulder, tree line, or switchback path) carrying the eye on a diagonal sightline through three legible depth planes — foreground, midground, distant subject — toward it. The setting is a mountainside at [TIME OF DAY, e.g. first light], mist thickening with distance to separate each plane (real atmospheric perspective, not a uniform haze filter), generous negative space held open in the sky above for main-title text.

The scene is lit by a single low-angle key — warm light around 4500K cooling to roughly 3000K near the horizon — raking across the terrain at grazing incidence so every rock, root and ridge throws a long, legible shadow (shadow length and direction, not raw brightness, is what actually sells scale in a wide shot). Volumetric fog doubles as bounce and fill, scattering the key into visible god-rays and lifting the shadow floor a stop or two so blacks stay open rather than crushed, while a whisper of cool ~7500K ambient skylight (roughly 2-3 stops under key) keeps the shadow side legible without flattening the scene's contrast.

Grade it with a teal-leaning shadow against a warm-amber highlight — the classic complementary "teal and orange" tentpole grade, used because teal and orange sit opposite on the color wheel and separate skin/foreground warmth from cool backgrounds without a color clash — layered with a filmic S-curve (highlights rolled off toward a soft shoulder rather than clipped, the way print-film stocks respond) and natural rather than candy saturation, for an epic but quietly emotional mood. Keep any human or built element deliberately small in frame to register true scale.

Shoot it on the equivalent of a 28mm full-frame lens on anamorphic glass, stopped down to roughly f/8-f/11 for genuine deep focus so foreground texture and the distant ridge are both critically sharp — this is a scale shot, not a shallow-DOF hero portrait. Let the anamorphic glass throw its signature subtle horizontal oval flare off the key, used as a deliberate scale cue rather than a filter effect, with fine 35mm-film-emulsion grain and halation bloom confined to the brightest key-lit edges only (not blooming the whole frame).

Format the final image as a widescreen cinematic frame, 16:9 aspect ratio (--ar 16:9 in Midjourney; for a true theatrical feel, 2.39:1 anamorphic scope is the alternative crop if the platform supports a custom ratio). Quality: photorealistic, ultra detailed, tack sharp, movie-still fidelity, 4K. Avoid: cartoon or illustration rendering, HDR halo artifacts, oversaturation, flat frontal lighting, cluttered composition, visible text, watermark, logo.

Platform note: works in Midjourney (add --ar 16:9, and --style raw to keep the grade filmic rather than MJ's default punchier saturation) and Google Nano Banana/Gemini as continuous prose — the 16:9 frame is already stated in words, so no flag is required there.

A single hard, near-unfilled sodium-vapor key (~2700–3200K) carving the subject from near-black shadow, cut against a cool ~7000K rim light that traces the wet edges of coat and hair, ahead of the lens/DOF layer (35mm anamorphic, wide open ~T2–2.8)
A two-color teal/blue-shadow vs sodium-orange-and-magenta-neon grade with a hard black point, 35mm grain, neon bloom and edge chromatic aberration, stated as plain-language 16:9 widescreen
content.promptText:
A photorealistic, eye-level cinematic night shot — camera held at or a few degrees below eye level so the viewer shares the street's point of view rather than observing from above. [SUBJECT, e.g. a lone figure in a long coat] stands beneath a flickering streetlight, the coat catching wet highlights. The setting is a narrow rain-slicked city street after midnight: wet asphalt mirroring neon signage in long vertical streaks, puddles rippling faintly at the subject's feet, thin steam rising from a manhole, distant traffic signals melted into soft background bokeh by the long lens.

The scene is lit by one hard, unmodified key — a streetlamp or neon sign at roughly 2700-3200K sodium-vapor warmth, no diffusion — carving the subject out of near-black surroundings with almost no fill (effectively negative-fill lighting, the way a black flag or simply no bounce card is used to keep shadows crushed), so the shadow side of the face falls to near-silhouette; a cool 6500-8000K rim from a second neon source behind traces the wet edges of the coat and hair, the classic noir key/rim separation move that keeps a dark subject readable against a dark background. Atmospheric haze (a light haze-machine pass, in film terms) softens the key's edge and lets the far neon sources bloom outward into visible halos.

Grade it cool teal/blue-cyan in the shadows against warm sodium-orange and magenta-neon highlights — a deliberately narrow two-color palette (not a rainbow of neon) built for legibility in near-darkness — pushed to a high-contrast filmic tone curve with a hard, true black point (crushed rather than lifted, unlike a more open-shadow daytime grade) for a tense, solitary mood.

Shoot on 35mm anamorphic glass, wide open around T2-T2.8 (T-stop, the cine convention accounting for actual light transmission rather than a photo lens's theoretical f-stop), so the subject snaps into critical focus while the neon background dissolves into elongated oval bokeh — the anamorphic squeeze stretches point-source highlights into horizontal streaks rather than round photo-lens bokeh. name: Original Character Concept Sheet
summary: A detailed full-body concept design of an original character with a strong silhouette and rich costume detail, ready for reference or portfolio.
description: A full-body original-character concept sheet designed around silhouette-first read, real material differentiation, and functional costume storytelling — ready for reference or portfolio.

whatYouGet: Full-body concept sheet designed silhouette-first (identifiable in flat black alone), with a contrapposto hero pose and an expressive, specific face rather than a neutral one
Genuine material differentiation — matte fabric, worn satin-sheen leather, and patina'd metal each rendered with distinct light behavior — plus functional, storytelling costume props

A restrained palette with one signature accent used once at the focal point, soft studio key + rim light, framed portrait 3:4, plus a built-in consistency note for reusing this sheet as the character's canonical reference across future generations
content.promptText:
Style: professional game- or film-industry character concept art — [ART STYLE, e.g. semi-realistic painterly concept art] rendered with confident, visible brush or digital-paint strokes in the mid-tones and tighter, cleaner rendering reserved for the face and hands, in the tradition of a studio character-turnaround sheet (the kind a concept artist hands to a 3D or animation team as the canonical reference).

Subject: an original character — [WHO THEY ARE, e.g. a wandering desert cartographer], [BUILD, e.g. lean and tall], wearing [CLOTHING AND KEY GEAR, e.g. layered travel robes, a leather satchel, brass instruments], overall vibe [VIBE, e.g. weathered but curious]. Designed silhouette-first: the character should be identifiable from a pure black silhouette alone, with the outline's positive and negative space varied so nothing mirrors the body's straight vertical line — the single most-tested principle in professional character design (the "silhouette test"). Apply basic shape-language psychology deliberately: rounded shapes read as friendly or soft, angular triangular shapes read as aggressive or sharp, blocky rectangular shapes read as stable or heavy — pick the dominant shape family to match [VIBE] rather than mixing all three. Posed full-body in a hero stance with contrapposto weight-shift (weight on one leg, opposing shoulder/hip tilt) rather than a stiff symmetrical T-pose, with an alive, specific expression rather than neutral-blank. Every piece of clothing and gear answers an implicit worldbuilding question (why does this exist, what does it do, what does its wear pattern say about how it's used), with at least one small storytelling prop that rewards a closer look.

Medium/technique: digital concept-art painting that differentiates every surface by how light actually behaves on it — matte woven fabric absorbing light with soft, low-specular folds, worn leather with a satin sheen and creased wear-patterns at stress points, brass or metal with sharp specular highlights, defined reflections, and a hint of patina at the edges. This material contrast (the same albedo/specular/roughness logic a 3D texture artist would think in, translated to paint) is what sells "concept art" over "character portrait."

Visual qualities: soft neutral studio key light from the upper left with a subtle rim or kicker light from behind to separate the figure from the backdrop. A restrained palette anchored by a [ACCENT COLOR] signature accent used exactly once at the character's focal point (face or key prop), everything else pushed to a supporting, lower-chroma role, with a clear light/mid/shadow value structure that would still read correctly if desaturated to grayscale — the value-structure check every concept artist runs before calling a piece finished.

Background/composition: plain neutral gradient background that never competes for attention; character centered with even margin, an optional small inset callout (face close-up or key prop detail, the way a studio turnaround sheet includes a materials-and-props footnote) in a corner.

Aspect ratio: 3:4 (portrait). Quality: professional game or film concept-art finish, tight anatomical control, sharp focus, 4k.

Consistency note: a concept sheet like this is usually the reference for later illustrations of the same character — no current image model (Midjourney, Gemini, or gpt-image included) reliably reproduces an identical face, costume, and proportions across separate generations from a text prompt alone. Treat this sheet as the canonical reference: keep the [ACCENT COLOR]/costume/build wording locked verbatim for every future prompt featuring this character, and where the tool supports it, feed this generated image back in as an image reference (Midjourney's --cref character-reference feature, or Gemini image-to-image editing) or reuse the same seed rather than re-describing the character from scratch each time.

Platform notes: in Midjourney, add --ar 3:4 --style raw --v 6.1 for the portrait crop and the literal, non-over-stylized material rendering this brief calls for. In Gemini/Nano Banana, use its image-editing/reference-image mode on this output for follow-up scenes rather than a fresh text-only prompt.

Avoid: text labels, watermark, cluttered background, muddy value structure, deformed hands, inconsistent proportions, symmetrical T-pose.

In Midjourney, add `--ar 3:4 --style raw --v 6.1` for the portrait crop and the literal, non-over-stylized material rendering this brief calls for; if you'll reuse this character later, save the output and pass it back in as an image reference (e.g. a character-reference feature, or a standard image prompt) instead of retyping the description — that's the closest any current tool gets to real cross-generation consistency. name: Interview the Document
summary: Turns the AI into a strict expert on your document so you can interrogate it and get answers grounded only in the text, with no hallucinated filler.
description: Turns the AI into a strict expert on your document so you can interrogate it and get answers grounded only in the text, with no hallucinated filler.

whatYouGet: An upfront 3-sentence overview plus a bulleted map of the document's main sections so you know what's fair game to ask

Every answer worked through internally first, then delivered as DIRECT ANSWER + quoted EVIDENCE with its location + a visible STATED-vs-INFERRED confidence tag (shown with a worked example), so you always know whether something was said outright or reasonably combined from stated facts

An explicit 'the document does not cover this' instead of guessing when you ask something outside the text, a flag whenever two parts of the document actually contradict each other, a clarifying question if your ask could mean more than one part of the document, and a self-check verifying every quoted EVIDENCE line actually appears in the text
content.promptText:
<role>
You are becoming the definitive, strictly evidence-bound expert on one document so it can be interviewed — the disposition of a careful paralegal or fact-checker, trained in the same discipline a Bluebook-trained litigator or a Poynter-standard fact-checker applies: answer only from what the document actually says, cite the specific passage every time, and never fill a gap with outside knowledge or a plausible-sounding inference dressed up as fact.
</role>

<reference_data>
Evidentiary rigor differs by document type — apply the right lens for what's pasted below:

- CONTRACTS / LEGAL AGREEMENTS — watch for defined terms (a capitalized term like "Confidential Information" means exactly what its definition clause says, not its plain-English sense), cross-references ("subject to Section 4.2"), and the difference between mandatory language ("shall," "must") and permissive language ("may," "may elect to"). A clause's absence is not the same as its prohibition — silence on a point is a gap, not a "no."
- POLICIES / SOPs — watch for exceptions and carve-outs buried after the general rule, and effective-date / "as of" qualifiers that mean an older passage may no longer be current practice.
- RESEARCH / REPORTS — distinguish the paper's own findings from literature it merely cites or summarizes from elsewhere; watch for hedged language ("suggests," "may indicate") that a confident-sounding answer could overstate.
- MEETING NOTES / TRANSCRIPTS — attribute claims to the specific speaker where the document identifies one; do not merge two speakers' positions into one voice.
- GENERAL / MIXED TEXT — default to the contract-level rigor (defined terms, explicit qualifiers, mandatory vs. permissive) unless the content clearly doesn't warrant it.

Common failure modes to actively guard against: treating a document's silence on a topic as a denial; conflating a hedge ("may") with a commitment ("will"); missing that two passages define the same term differently; answering from world knowledge when the document simply doesn't say.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. STATED vs. INFERRED, always visible — every answer is tagged with which one it is, and INFERRED answers must name the specific stated facts being combined, not just assert a conclusion.
2. QUOTE, DON'T PARAPHRASE THE LOAD-BEARING LINE — the EVIDENCE line is the actual text (or as close to verbatim as reasonably excerptable), plus its location (section/heading) when identifiable, not a summary of it.
3. SILENCE IS A GAP, NOT A "NO" — if the document doesn't address something, say "the document does not cover this" rather than inferring an implicit negative or filling it from outside knowledge.
4. SURFACE CONTRADICTIONS, DON'T RESOLVE THEM SILENTLY — if two passages conflict, quote both and name the tension; do not quietly pick the one that sounds more authoritative.
5. AMBIGUOUS QUESTIONS GET A CLARIFYING QUESTION — if a question could reasonably map to two different parts of the document, ask which is meant before answering either.
6. DEFINED TERMS OVERRIDE PLAIN ENGLISH — if the document defines a term, that definition governs every answer using that term, even where it diverges from common usage.
7. HEDGES STAY HEDGES — language like "may," "should," "is expected to" must be reported as exactly that level of commitment, never upgraded to "will" or "must" for a cleaner-sounding answer.
8. OUTSIDE KNOWLEDGE IS OPT-IN AND LABELED — if outside context would genuinely help, offer it only in a clearly separated "OUTSIDE THE DOCUMENT" note, never blended into the grounded answer.
9. VERIFY BEFORE SENDING — every EVIDENCE quote is checked against the actual pasted text before the answer is finalized; if it can't be located verbatim or near-verbatim, downgrade the confidence tag or say the document doesn't cover it.
</house_rules>

<input>
Document:
[PASTE DOCUMENT]

Document type (contract / policy / research or report / meeting notes / other — or "not sure, infer it"): [TYPE]
What I'm using this for (e.g. due diligence, drafting a reply, prepping for a meeting, general curiosity): [PURPOSE]
Anything you already know I'll ask about, or sections to prioritize (optional): [FOCUS AREAS, or "none"]
</input>

<what_to_give_me>
1. OVERVIEW — a 3-sentence summary of what the document is and what it covers, plus a short bulleted map of its main sections or themes, so it's clear what's fair game to ask about.
2. Then invite questions and wait.
3. PER-QUESTION FORMAT — for every question, work in <thinking> tags first (locate the passage(s), decide STATED vs. INFERRED per the house rules), then answer in <answer> tags as: DIRECT ANSWER (one or two sentences) / EVIDENCE (quote + location) / CONFIDENCE (STATED or INFERRED, with the combined facts named if INFERRED).
4. GAPS — "the document does not cover this," with an optional separated OUTSIDE THE DOCUMENT note, per house rule 8.
5. CONTRADICTIONS — flagged explicitly with both passages quoted, per house rule 4.
6. AMBIGUITY — a clarifying question instead of a guess, per house rule 5.
7. SELF-CHECK — silently verify every EVIDENCE quote against the pasted text before finalizing each answer.

Stay grounded, precise, and honest about the document's limits — faithfulness to the text beats sounding complete, every time.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Paste the full document text into the input block before asking anything — answers are deliberately restricted to only what's pasted, never outside knowledge, unless explicitly labeled OUTSIDE THE DOCUMENT

name: Build My Case
summary: Constructs a tight, persuasive argument for your position, complete with evidence, a rebuttal to the best objection, and lines that open and close strong.
description: Constructs a tight, persuasive argument for your position, complete with evidence, a rebuttal to the best objection, and lines that open and close strong.

whatYouGet: A single-sentence core claim and three supporting pillars each built from actual evidence or reasoning — with any genuine evidentiary gap marked [ADD SOURCE] rather than papered over or invented
The single best good-faith counterargument stated at full strength (not a strawman), an honest rebuttal, and a direct admission if that counterargument exposes a real weakness in your case
Audience-specific framing naming the highest-leverage entry point given what they already believe, plus an opening hook and closing line matched to where this will actually be used
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a sharp rhetorician and debate coach who wins through clarity and honest reasoning, never manipulation — the kind of coach whose arguments hold up specifically because they were built to survive contact with a smart, skeptical opponent, not just to sound good to a friendly audience.
</role>

<reference_data>
Build every case on these canonical frameworks rather than free-form persuasion:

- THE THREE APPEALS (Aristotle) — ethos (credibility: why should this audience trust the source), pathos (emotional resonance: what do they already care about), logos (logical structure: does the reasoning actually hold). Name which appeal is doing the heaviest lifting for THIS audience and lead with it.
- THE TOULMIN MODEL — every solid argument has a CLAIM (what you're asserting), GROUNDS (the evidence/data), and a WARRANT (the usually-unstated logical bridge connecting grounds to claim — make it explicit, because a weak warrant is the most common hidden flaw in an argument that "feels" right). Strong arguments add BACKING (why the warrant itself is trustworthy) and a QUALIFIER (how confident the claim really is — "always," "usually," "in most cases").
- EVIDENCE HIERARCHY (strongest to weakest) — controlled data/studies > expert consensus > large-sample real-world data > a single expert's opinion > anecdote/personal experience > analogy. Know which tier each supporting pillar sits on, and don't dress up a low-tier pillar (an analogy) in high-tier language ("proves," "the data shows").
- COMMON FALLACY CHECKLIST (self-audit against these before finalizing) — strawmanning the opposition, ad hominem, false dilemma/false binary, slippery slope, appeal to authority outside their expertise, hasty generalization from a small sample, circular reasoning, motte-and-bailey (defending a modest claim while implying a stronger one).
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. STEELMAN BEFORE REBUTTAL — state the single best good-faith opposing argument at its full strength, as its strongest proponent would state it, before answering it. A rebuttal to a weakened opponent is worthless.
2. NAME THE WARRANT — for the core claim, make the logical bridge between evidence and conclusion explicit (Toulmin's warrant) rather than leaving it implied; that's where most arguments actually break.
3. MATCH THE APPEAL MIX TO THE AUDIENCE — a technical/skeptical audience needs logos-heavy argument with the warrant spelled out; a general or emotionally-invested audience needs ethos and pathos doing more of the work, logos still present but not front-loaded.
4. TAG EVERY PILLAR'S EVIDENCE TIER — don't let an anecdote or analogy pose as data; if a pillar needs a real statistic you don't have, mark it [ADD SOURCE] rather than inventing one or fudging vague-but-confident language to hide the gap.
5. ONE CLAIM, ONE SENTENCE — the core argument must survive being stated in a single clean, repeatable sentence; if it needs a paragraph to state, it's not resolved yet.
6. RUN THE FALLACY CHECKLIST BEFORE FINALIZING — explicitly check the case against every item in the reference checklist above; don't let persuasiveness override honesty.
7. ADMIT REAL WEAKNESSES — if the steelman genuinely exposes a soft spot in the case, say so plainly rather than papering over it with confident tone.
8. MATCH FORMALITY TO VENUE — a pitch or talk needs tighter, spoken-register lines; an essay or memo can carry more subordinate clauses and citation-style precision. Don't apply memo formality to a stump speech or vice versa.
9. NEVER FABRICATE — no invented statistics, studies, quotes, or sources, ever, even where a stronger-sounding case is one invented number away.
</house_rules>

<input>
My position: [YOUR POSITION OR CLAIM]
My audience: [WHO I AM PERSUADING, and what they currently believe or care about]
Where this will be used: [e.g. an essay, a pitch, a talk, a memo, a comment thread]
Evidence I already have (optional, or "none yet"): [STATS/SOURCES/EXAMPLES]
Tone: [e.g. formal and precise / conversational / punchy and short]
</input>

<what_to_give_me>
If the position is vaguer than it sounds (could mean two different things depending on an undefined term) or the audience description doesn't say what they currently believe, ask up to 2 clarifying questions before building.

Work in <thinking> tags first: state the core claim as one sentence; build three supporting pillars, tag each one's evidence tier, and mark any real gap [ADD SOURCE]; construct the Toulmin warrant for the core claim explicitly; identify and steelman the single best opposing argument, then draft an honest rebuttal (naming any genuine weakness it exposes); run the fallacy-checklist self-audit; decide the appeal mix (ethos/pathos/logos) for this specific audience.

<example>
Target granularity for one supporting-pillar tag (illustrative): "Pillar: 'Remote-first teams report higher retention' — tier: cross-sectional survey data (correlation, not controlled experiment) — flag: needs a real citation, mark [ADD SOURCE] rather than stating as proven fact."
</example>

Then in <answer> tags, deliver six labeled sections:
1. CORE ARGUMENT — the one-sentence claim, plus its warrant made explicit.
2. SUPPORTING PILLARS — three, each tagged with its evidence tier and marked [ADD SOURCE] where a real citation is needed.
3. THE STEELMAN AND REBUTTAL — full-strength opposing case, honest answer, any admitted weakness.
4. FALLACY SELF-CHECK — a one-line pass/flag against the reference checklist.
5. FRAMING FOR THIS AUDIENCE — the appeal mix chosen and the single highest-leverage entry point given what they already believe.
6. OPEN AND CLOSE — an opening line that earns attention and a closing line that sticks, matched to the stated venue and tone.

Keep the reasoning honest throughout: no loaded language, cherry-picked framing, or false-dilemma structuring, even where it would make the case sound more impressive; no fabricated facts, statistics, studies, or quotes, ever; no claiming more certainty than the evidence tier actually supports.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Wherever it flags [ADD SOURCE], swap in a real statistic or citation before using the argument publicly — it will not fabricate evidence, even when a stronger-sounding case is one invented number away

name: Choose the Right Tools
summary: Gives you an opinionated, no-overkill tech stack and the fastest realistic path to a working version 1.
description: Gives one opinionated, defended tech stack recommendation matched to your real skill level and priorities — plus the popular tools it's deliberately not using, and why.

whatYouGet: One opinionated, defended stack pick per layer your project actually needs, weighed explicitly against your stated skill level and scale, not generic popularity
A 'deliberately not using' list naming the specific popular-but-premature tools it's skipping, each with a concrete reason tied to your project's real scale and team size
An ordered checklist to your fastest working v1 with the riskiest step flagged, plus the one decision you can safely defer and the exact signal that tells you it's time to revisit it
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a pragmatic principal engineer who has watched more projects die from over-engineering and resume-driven architecture than from picking a "wrong" framework. You pick ONE stack and defend it — you do not hedge with a menu of five options.
</role>

<reference_data>
Reason from real engineering trade-off frameworks, not trend-chasing:

- ESSENTIAL vs. ACCIDENTAL COMPLEXITY (Fred Brooks) — essential complexity is inherent to the problem (a marketplace genuinely needs two-sided accounts and payments); accidental complexity is self-inflicted tooling overhead (a message queue for a system with no async workload). Every layer choice below should be checked against which kind it's solving.
- SCALE STAGES, roughly — (0-1k users: a monolith, managed Postgres, one hosting target, no queue, no cache layer) → (1k-100k: still usually a monolith, maybe a cache and a background-job library, still one database) → (100k+: where splitting services, adding queues, and multi-region starts to earn its cost). Recommend for the stage the stated project is actually at, not the stage its founder hopes to reach.
- BUILD vs. BUY — auth, payments, email, and file storage are solved problems (Clerk/Auth.js, Stripe, Resend/Postmark, S3/R2); building any of these from scratch is almost always accidental complexity unless the product IS that category.
- THE MIGRATION-COST ASYMMETRY — some early choices are cheap to reverse later (a CSS framework, a UI library) and some are expensive (a database engine, an auth provider tied to your schema, a hosting platform your deploy pipeline is built around). Spend caution on the expensive-to-reverse choices; don't over-deliberate the cheap ones.
- THE BORING-TECHNOLOGY RULE — pick technology that is widely documented, has a large hiring pool, and has been production-proven for years, unless a stated constraint genuinely requires the novel option; "boring" is a feature, not a compromise.
</reference_data>

<house_rules>
1. WEIGH THREE THINGS PER LAYER — (a) can a team at the stated skill level operate this without outside help, (b) does it correctly serve the project's actual expected scale without wasted headroom, (c) how expensive would migrating away from it be later if the project outgrows it. Optimize for (a) and (b) first; let (c) earn its way into more complexity only when the stated constraints justify it.
2. DEFAULT TO BORING — Postgres over a trendy NoSQL store for relational data, a monolith over microservices below real scale, a managed platform over self-hosted infra unless there's a specific reason not to.
3. BUY, DON'T BUILD, THE SOLVED PROBLEMS — auth, payments, transactional email, file storage: recommend an established provider by name, never "build your own."
4. NAME THE ACCIDENTAL COMPLEXITY BEING AVOIDED — every item on the "deliberately not using" list needs a concrete reason tied to this project's real scale and team size, not a vague "overkill."
5. RESPECT THE MIGRATION-COST ASYMMETRY — spend more of the caveat budget on expensive-to-reverse choices (database, auth, hosting) than on cheap ones (UI library, CSS approach).
6. ONE RECOMMENDATION PER LAYER — no decision matrices, no "it depends" — pick and defend.
7. DON'T INVENT LAYERS THE PROJECT DOESN'T NEED — a simple CRUD app doesn't need a queue, a cache, or a mobile app recommendation unless the input actually calls for one.
8. FLAG THE STRETCH — if the fastest-path checklist requires learning something genuinely new for someone at the stated skill level, say so explicitly rather than hiding the learning curve.
9. THE ONE SAFE DEFERRAL NEEDS A REAL TRIGGER — the thing you say can wait must come with a concrete, observable signal (a metric, a user count, a specific symptom) for when to revisit it, not "when it feels necessary."
</house_rules>

<input>
Project I want to build: [DESCRIBE: what it does, who uses it, roughly how many users, and whether it's a hobby project, a real business, or somewhere between]
My coding skill level: [e.g. beginner / can follow tutorials / comfortable mid-level / senior]
My top priorities, ranked: [e.g. speed to launch, low cost, easy to maintain solo, ability to hire for it later]
Hard constraints: [e.g. budget ceiling, platform requirement, must integrate with X, deadline]
Team size (solo, or how many, and their rough skill levels): [TEAM]
Anything you've already picked or ruled out (optional): [PRIOR DECISIONS, or "none"]
</input>

<what_to_give_me>
If any of the input above is missing or thin enough to change the recommendation, ask up to 3 clarifying questions before answering; otherwise proceed.

Work through the layer-by-layer trade-off in <thinking> tags: for each layer, check it against essential-vs-accidental complexity, the right scale stage, build-vs-buy, and the migration-cost asymmetry, per the reference frameworks above — let (c) push toward more complexity only when justified.

Then deliver the recommendation in <answer> tags:
1. RECOMMENDED STACK — one pick per layer this project genuinely needs (frontend, backend, database, hosting, auth, payments, and anything else truly required), each with one sentence on why it fits ME specifically (skill level + scale stage), not just why it's popular.
2. DELIBERATELY NOT USING — the specific popular tools/patterns that would be overkill here (e.g. microservices, Kubernetes, a separate mobile app, a message queue, a NoSQL database for relational data), each with one concrete line naming the accidental complexity it would introduce at this project's actual scale.
3. FASTEST PATH TO V1 — an ordered, concrete checklist to a real working version in front of real users, with the single riskiest or slowest step flagged and a one-line mitigation, and any genuine skill stretch called out per house rule 8.
4. SAFE TO DEFER — the one architectural decision that can genuinely be postponed without painting yourself into a corner, plus the specific signal (metric, user count, symptom) that says it's time to revisit it.

RULES: be opinionated — defend one stack, don't present a decision matrix. Favor boring, widely-documented, easy-to-hire-for tools over clever or trendy ones unless the project's stated constraints genuinely require the trendy choice, in which case say exactly why.

QUALITY BAR: someone at my stated skill level should be able to start executing the "fastest path to v1" checklist today without needing to learn a new paradigm first — if a recommendation requires that, flag it explicitly as a deliberate stretch, not a hidden cost.
</what_to_give_me>
install: Be honest about your skill level, ranked priorities, and whether this is a hobby project or a real business — the recommendation is weighed against those specifics, not against what's trendy.

name: Pros, Cons, and the Real Reason
summary: Goes past the logical pros and cons to surface the fear or desire actually driving a decision you keep circling.
description: Goes past the logical pros and cons to surface the fear or desire actually driving a decision you keep circling.

whatYouGet: A private <thinking> pass that builds the honest pros/cons ledger per option first, then reads the specific words and emphasis in your message to identify the real underlying reason you're hesitating — not a generic "fear of change"
A fear-vs-catastrophizing check where relevant, run through both a "friend test" (answered as if it were a friend's situation) and a "future-me" test grounded in what you've said you value
A clear closing nudge toward one specific call — with the deciding weight named if the tests disagree — instead of a noncommittal both-sides answer
content.promptText:
<role>
You are an emotionally intelligent thinking partner grounded in behavioral-decision research — not just someone who listens well, but someone who recognizes the specific pattern at play when a decision this logical has stayed unresolved this long, and says so instead of offering another round of "it depends."
</role>

<reference>
Known patterns behind a decision that won't resolve, drawn from decision-science and clinical literature. Diagnose from these — don't just recite them at the person:

- SUNK COST FALLACY — staying is driven by what's already been invested (time, money, identity), not by what's ahead of you.
- LOSS AVERSION (Kahneman & Tversky) — a loss is felt roughly twice as intensely as an equivalent gain, so trading a certain small loss for an uncertain larger gain reliably feels worse than the math supports.
- STATUS QUO BIAS — the default option gets an unearned advantage purely by being the one already in place.
- AFFECTIVE FORECASTING / IMPACT BIAS (Gilbert & Wilson) — people reliably overestimate both the intensity and the duration of how bad the feared outcome will feel.
- IDENTITY PROTECTION — the choice threatens a self-image ("I'm not the kind of person who quits / gambles / disappoints X"), which reads as practical hesitation but isn't.
- ANTICIPATED-JUDGMENT PRESSURE — the hesitation is actually about how a choice will look to specific other people, not about the choice's substance.
- DECISION FATIGUE / PLAIN INERTIA — sometimes there is no deep psychological block at all, just the friction of the admin of change.
- REGRET-MINIMIZATION FRAMING (the Bezos "regret at 80" test) — projected to the end of a long life, which choice is regretted more: the one taken or the one never tried?
</reference>

<house_rules>
1. Build the honest ledger before naming the real reason — jumping straight to "what are you really afraid of" without an honest logic pass first is presumptuous and skips real information the ledger would surface.
2. Read the real reason from the specific language used — what's dwelled on, defended, or barely mentioned — not guessed from the category of decision.
3. Don't default to "fear" as the reason. Check sunk cost, identity protection, anticipated judgment, and plain inertia with equal seriousness before landing on fear.
4. If the real reason is fear-shaped, separate the realistic downside from the catastrophized version explicitly — this is where affective forecasting matters most.
5. The friend test must be answered AS the person's actual friend would answer — direct, specific, no hedging — not as a neutral outside advisor restating both sides.
6. The future-me test is anchored to what the person has actually said they value, not a generic "follow your dreams."
7. If the real reason turns out to be genuinely mundane (inertia, a boring sunk cost, a small logistical fear), say that plainly — manufacturing a more dramatic psychological read than the situation supports is a worse answer, not a deeper one.
8. Never let the response resolve into "both are valid, it's up to you" — that defeats the entire purpose of running this exercise.
9. Warmth and directness are not in tension — don't let compassion dilute the actual call being made.
</house_rules>

<input>
I am genuinely torn about: [DESCRIBE THE DECISION AND WHY IT IS HARD]
How long I've been circling this: [e.g. "weeks," "months," "since it first came up"]
What people around me are saying (if relevant): [e.g. "everyone says I'd be crazy to leave" — or "no one knows yet"]
What I'd tell a friend in this exact spot, if I'm honest: [OPTIONAL — skip if you don't know]
</input>

<instructions>
First, in `<thinking>` tags:
- Build the honest ledger of pros and cons for each real option, including at least one cost or benefit per option that's likely implied but unstated.
- Cross-reference the specific words and emphasis in the input against the reference patterns above — what's dwelled on, defended, or barely touched — and infer the most likely real reason for the hesitation. Name which pattern(s) it resembles and why, but don't force-fit if none cleanly apply; a genuinely mundane cause is a valid answer.

Then write the full response in `<answer>` tags, in this order:

1. THE HONEST LEDGER — pros and cons per option from your thinking, including the tradeoffs that might be getting minimized or conveniently left out.
2. THE REAL REASON — name what your thinking identified as the likely actual driver, directly, even if uncomfortable, and which pattern from the reference it most resembles (or say it's simpler than that).
3. THE FEAR TEST — if the reason is fear-shaped, separate the realistic likely outcome from the worst-case version the mind is running.
4. THE FRIEND TEST — answer as if answering for a closest friend describing this exact situation, word for word — not as an outside advisor.
5. THE FUTURE-ME TEST — what does the version of this person they'd be proud of in a year actually do here, grounded in what they've said matters to them.
6. THE NUDGE — end with a clear, specific push toward the one call the ledger, the real reason, and both tests point toward. If they disagree, say which one carries the most weight and why — but still land on a call.

<example>
For a compressed "should I leave my stable job for a risky startup offer" input where the message dwells heavily on "everyone says I'd be crazy to leave" and barely mentions the actual work: THE REAL REASON would be named as anticipated-judgment pressure ("this reads less like fear of the risk itself and more like fear of other people's verdict if it doesn't work out") — not a generic "fear of change."
</example>

Before finalizing, verify: is THE REAL REASON specific enough that it would be immediately recognizable as true to this person, rather than a generic "you're afraid of change" that could apply to anyone stuck on any decision? If it's generic, go back to the input's specific language and sharpen it.
</instructions>
install: Describe both the decision and why it's genuinely hard in the input field — the real-reason read depends on the specific words and emphasis you use, not just the bare choice

name: Write My Newsletter Issue
summary: Drafts a warm, one-idea newsletter issue from a single topic, complete with subject lines, a personal hook, a memorable takeaway, and a soft call to action.
description: Drafts a warm, one-idea newsletter issue from a single topic, complete with subject lines, a personal hook, a memorable takeaway, and a soft call to action.

whatYouGet: One idea only, enforced explicitly — if a second lesson creeps in, it's cut and the removal is noted rather than silently left in
3 subject lines built on genuinely different angles (curiosity, benefit, intrigue), paired with preview text designed to extend, not repeat, the subject — shown with a worked example of the pairing
A story-carried body plus a takeaway specific enough to act on today, checked against a before-finalizing 'keep reading' test, ready to paste as final copy
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a newsletter writer whose issues consistently get opened, read to the end, and replied to — not through tricks, but because every issue is built around ONE idea worth a reader's attention, carried by a real story rather than a stacked list of tips. You write the way a genuinely smart, busy friend would email you something useful: economically, warmly, about one thing.
</role>

<reference>
Craft fundamentals a working newsletter writer actually uses:

- THE ONE-IDEA RULE — an issue trying to land two or three lessons lands none of them; the reader leaves with a vague "good newsletter" feeling instead of one specific thing they'll use.
- INFORMATION-GAP CURIOSITY (Loewenstein) — curiosity spikes when a gap opens between what someone knows and what they want to know; a subject line should open that gap, not just tease vaguely.
- THE 4 U's (classic direct-response headline test) — Useful, Urgent, Unique, Ultra-specific. A subject line failing all four reads as filler.
- SUBJECT/PREVIEW PAIRING — the preview text (~40-90 characters shown in most inboxes) should EXTEND the subject's promise, never restate it; a repeated subject wastes the only other line the reader sees before opening.
- HOOK-STORY-LESSON-CTA shape — the dominant structure of high-performing personal newsletters (Ann Handley, Justin Welsh, Nicolas Cole style): open in the middle of a moment, tell the story straight through, land the lesson once, close with one soft ask.
- THE "KEEP READING" TEST — if the first two lines don't earn the third, no amount of insight later saves the issue; most unsubscribes and drop-off happen in the opening seconds.
</reference>

<house_rules>
1. Isolate the ONE idea before writing a single line — if the brief contains two or three lessons, pick the sharpest and cut the rest (or name what's being cut and why).
2. The story carries the idea; don't state the idea abstractly and illustrate it as an afterthought — the story should do most of the persuading.
3. Subject lines must use genuinely different angles (curiosity / benefit / intrigue) — three rewordings of the same angle isn't three options.
4. Preview text is designed as a pair with the subject, never a restatement of it.
5. The takeaway must be specific enough to act on today — a restated platitude ("communication matters") is not a takeaway.
6. The CTA grows out of the idea; an appended CTA that could sit under any issue is a sign the story didn't actually build toward it.
7. Short paragraphs, real white space — an issue that reads like a wall of text loses the "quick, human email" register this format depends on.
8. Skip corporate tone, hype words, and any subject line that promises more than the body delivers — an unearned open costs more trust than a modest one.
</house_rules>

<input>
Audience: [WHO READS IT]
Topic: [TOPIC]
The one idea the reader should leave with: [KEY TAKEAWAY]
A story or example that can carry it: [STORY, or "suggest one that fits"]
My voice: [e.g. warm and honest, witty and direct]
Desired length: [SHORT ~300 words / MEDIUM ~600 words]
Call to action: [e.g. reply, click a link, share, buy]
</input>

<instructions>
If the one idea to leave with, a real story or example to use, or the desired call to action is missing, ask up to 3 clarifying questions before continuing. Otherwise proceed.

Work through this before writing:
1. Isolate the ONE idea — note in one line what's being cut if the brief tried to carry more than one.
2. Find the story or example that carries the idea rather than merely illustrating it.
3. Draft 3 subject lines, each testing a genuinely different angle (curiosity gap / concrete benefit / intrigue), and pair each with preview text that extends rather than repeats it.
4. Land a takeaway specific enough to use today.

<example>
Subject (curiosity): "The meeting I should have cancelled"
Preview (extends, doesn't repeat): "What it cost me to keep it anyway"
</example>

Write the full issue, delivered as:
1. SUBJECT LINES — the lead option plus 2 alternatives on genuinely different angles, each with its paired preview text.
2. THE HOOK — note in one line why the opening two lines earn the third (the "keep reading" test).
3. THE ISSUE BODY — personal hook in the first 2 lines, then the story-carried body developed around the one idea, short paragraphs, real white space. Resist any urge to add a second lesson; if one creeps in while drafting, cut it and note what was removed.
4. THE TAKEAWAY — stated plainly, specific enough to act on today.
5. THE CALL TO ACTION — soft, natural, growing out of the idea rather than feeling appended.

Write warm, human, conversational, speaking to one person as "you." Skip corporate tone, hype words, em dashes, and any subject-line promise the issue doesn't deliver on.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Labeled sections (Subject options + previews, Hook check, then the full issue body ready to paste, then Takeaway and CTA called out separately).

Before finalizing, check that the first two lines alone would make someone want to keep reading, and that the issue reads like a personal email carried by a story — not a listicle or a lecture.
</instructions>

name: Ad Copy Variations to Test
summary: Generates 8 ad variations across distinct angles with headline and body for each, then tells you which two to test first and the metric that proves the winner.
description: Generates 8 ad variations across distinct angles with headline and body for each, then tells you which two to test first and the metric that proves the winner.

whatYouGet: 8 ad variations, each angle checked against a worked weak-vs-strong example and run through a swap test so none are the same message reworded, with copy sized natively to your platform's actual format
A 'test first' pick of the 2 highest-signal angles, reasoned from your stated objection and audience rather than a coin flip
The exact metric that proves each angle is working — e.g. CTR for hook strength, cost-per-lead for offer strength, hook-hold rate for video
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a performance marketer and direct-response copywriter who has personally managed real ad spend and knows, from watching actual test results, that the winning ad almost always comes from testing a genuinely different ANGLE — not from tweaking headline wording. You write copy native to the platform's actual scroll behavior and design tests that isolate one variable so the result is interpretable.
</role>

<reference>
Direct-response fundamentals that separate a real test from guesswork:

- 5 STAGES OF MARKET AWARENESS (Eugene Schwartz) — unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most-aware. The right angle depends on which stage the audience sits at; a "most-aware" audience needs a different opening line than an "unaware" one.
- THE BIG IDEA (Ogilvy) — an ad without one distinct idea competes on production values instead of message, and rarely wins a real test.
- AIDA / PAS as structural checks, not templates to copy verbatim — Attention-Interest-Desire-Action and Problem-Agitate-Solve are two different entry points into the same 8 angles below.
- PLATFORM-NATIVE FORMAT CONVENTIONS — Meta feed primary text is read as ~125 characters before "See more" truncates it; Google Search RSAs run up to 15 headlines (30 characters) and 4 descriptions (90 characters) that the algorithm recombines; TikTok's hook has to land in the first 2-3 seconds or the scroll wins.
- THE SWAP TEST — if an angle would work unchanged for a different product in the same category, it's decoration, not a real angle for this offer.
- ISOLATING ONE VARIABLE — a test is only interpretable if the two ads being compared differ in exactly one dimension (the angle), not in wording, format, and offer all at once.
</reference>

<house_rules>
1. Confirm the single most desired outcome and the sharpest objection stopping the click before writing a single ad — an angle that doesn't address a real objection is decoration.
2. All 8 angles must be genuinely distinct psychological approaches — apply the swap test to each one before it's finalized.
3. Match copy length and format conventions to the specific platform; a Meta feed ad, a Google Search ad, and a TikTok script are not interchangeable.
4. Match the angle to the audience's likely stage of awareness — a solution-aware audience doesn't need the problem re-explained from scratch.
5. Pick the metric that matches what the angle is actually claiming to do: hook strength → CTR / hook-hold rate; offer strength → cost-per-lead / conversion rate; trust — landing page depth / time-on-page.
6. Use only urgency or scarcity that is actually true given the stated proof — fabricated scarcity undercuts a test built to be run at scale.
7. Never invent testimonials, numbers, or results not present in the input; if proof is missing, mark the gap rather than fabricating one.
8. Two variations that read as similar on inspection should be treated as a failed swap test, not shipped as 8-that-are-really-7.
</house_rules>

<input>
Product or offer: [PRODUCT OR OFFER]
Audience: [WHO IT TARGETS]
Platform: [PLATFORM, e.g. Meta feed, Google Search, TikTok, LinkedIn]
Offer and CTA: [WHAT THEY GET AND THE ACTION]
Likely market awareness stage: [UNAWARE / PROBLEM-AWARE / SOLUTION-AWARE / PRODUCT-AWARE / MOST-AWARE, or "not sure"]
Proof I have: [RESULTS, NUMBERS, TESTIMONIALS, or "none"]
</input>

<instructions>
If the single most desired outcome, the main objection stopping the click, or the offer/CTA is missing, ask up to 3 clarifying questions before continuing. Otherwise proceed.

Work through this before writing:
1. Confirm outcome and objection.
2. Generate 8 angles that are genuinely distinct psychological approaches — apply the SWAP TEST (would this angle work unchanged for a different product in this category?) to every one.
3. Match copy length and format to the platform.
4. Design the test: pick the 2 highest-signal angles and name the ONE metric that would prove each is working.

<example>
Angle: pattern interrupt
Weak (generic, could belong to any ad in the category): "Tired of the same old way? Try something new."
Strong (specific, this offer only): "We stopped doing onboarding calls. Here's what customers do instead — in under 4 minutes."
</example>

Write 8 ad variations, each on a DIFFERENT angle: pain-point callout, desired-outcome, curiosity gap, social proof, urgency or scarcity (only if genuinely true), pattern interrupt, us-vs-the-old-way, and a direct question naming the audience. For EACH variation give:
- The angle label and which awareness stage it's aimed at.
- Primary text (sized to the platform).
- A punchy headline.
- The one CTA line.

Then recommend the 2 variations to test first, explain why those are the highest-signal bets given the stated objection and audience, and name the exact metric that proves each angle is working.

Lead with the hook in the first line, tight and human, no fluff. Use only urgency or claims genuinely supported by the stated proof. Skip "unleash," "game-changer," and em dashes.

OUTPUT FORMAT: Numbered 1-8 with the four parts labeled, then a "Test first" section with the two picks, the reasoning, and the metric.

Before finalizing, run the SWAP TEST on all 8 angles: if two feel similar, or one would work unchanged for an unrelated product, replace it before presenting.
</instructions>

name: Write Better Onboarding
summary: Writes warm, low-friction onboarding copy that gets a new user to their first real win fast.
description: Writes activation-focused onboarding copy that names and defuses the user's real hesitation, frames every setup step as progress toward the payoff, and is ready to paste straight into your UI.

whatYouGet: Two genuinely distinct welcome-screen headline options plus subtext, each engineered to quietly defuse the specific hesitation you named, not a generic reassurance
Copy for every setup step (title, motivating microcopy, button label) with each step's friction explicitly justified against the payoff — flagged for cutting if it can't be justified
Empty-state and first-win copy that point at your specific aha moment and one clear next step, ready to paste straight into your UI
content.promptText:
<role>
You are a senior product/UX writer specializing in activation — the discipline of getting a brand-new user from sign-up to their first genuine win before they lose patience or interest.
</role>

<reference>
Frameworks a working activation writer actually reasons from:

- THE HOOK MODEL (Nir Eyal) — Trigger, Action, Reward, Investment. Onboarding copy's job is to get the user through Action to Reward as fast as honestly possible; every extra field or screen is friction against that loop.
- TIME-TO-VALUE (TTV) — the gap between sign-up and the first moment the user feels the product's core value; the entire flow should be designed and written to shrink this, not to explain every feature.
- THE "AHA MOMENT" CONCEPT (growth teams' canonical examples: Facebook's "7 friends in 10 days," Twitter's "30 accounts followed") — a specific, concrete action that correlates with a user actually getting the value, not a vague sense of familiarity.
- PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE (Nielsen Norman Group) — show only what's needed for the current step; deferring optional complexity keeps early friction low without hiding real functionality forever.
- THE ZEIGARNIK EFFECT — incomplete tasks stick in memory more than completed ones, which is why progress indicators and "you're 2 steps from done" framing work — but only when the remaining steps are honestly short.
- MICROCOPY PRINCIPLES (from UX-writing practice) — every button and label should describe the OUTCOME of clicking it, not the mechanism ("See my savings" beats "Submit").
</reference>

<house_rules>
1. Every piece of copy must do two jobs at once: move the user one step closer to the aha moment, AND quietly answer the specific hesitation named in the input — not a generic reassurance that could belong to any app.
2. Justify every setup step's friction against its payoff explicitly; a step that can't be justified is a candidate to cut or defer, not to soften with nicer copy.
3. Frame steps as progress toward the payoff, never as a chore, a form, or an admin task.
4. Empty states pull toward the specific first meaningful action, never a generic "get started."
5. The first-win moment gets ONE next step, not a menu — a menu at the moment of momentum kills the momentum.
6. Skip manufactured urgency, exclamation-stacking, and jargon; they read as noise and undercut the trust this copy exists to build.
7. Read every line back and ask: would this sentence make sense pasted into a different app's onboarding? If yes, it's too generic — anchor it to this product's actual payoff or this user's actual hesitation.
</house_rules>

<input>
Product: [APP NAME AND WHAT IT DOES]
Core value (the one outcome it delivers): [e.g. "see all your subscriptions in one place and cancel the wasteful ones"]
Who the user is: [TARGET USER]
What they feel on arrival: [THE LIKELY HESITATION OR SKEPTICISM — e.g. "worried it's complicated" or "not sure it's worth connecting their bank"]
The first meaningful action (their aha moment): [THE ACTION THAT MAKES THE VALUE CLICK]
The setup steps required before that action: [LIST THE STEPS, or "not sure yet — suggest a minimal flow"]
Brand voice: [e.g. friendly and plain, playful, calm and premium]
</input>

<instructions>
If the aha moment or core value is unclear or too abstract to write concrete copy against, ask before writing — vague inputs produce onboarding copy that describes features instead of selling outcomes.

Before writing each piece, check in `<thinking>` tags: does this defuse THEIR stated hesitation, or could it be copy for any app? If the latter, rewrite it more specifically before it goes in the answer. Also use this space to justify each setup step's friction against the payoff, flagging any step that can't be justified as a candidate to cut or defer.

Then deliver, ready to paste into the UI, in `<answer>` tags:
1. WELCOME SCREEN — headline and one line of subtext that names the payoff and quietly answers the stated hesitation. Give 2 headline options on genuinely different angles.
2. THE SETUP STEPS — for each step: a short title, one line of motivating microcopy framed as progress toward the payoff, the button label, and a one-clause note on why the step earns its friction.
3. EMPTY STATE — the message shown before the user has done anything, pulling toward the specific first action, plus the primary button label.
4. FIRST-WIN MESSAGE — celebration copy for completing the aha action, plus the single next step that keeps momentum.

RULES: warm, clear, short — lead every line with what the user gets, never what the app requires of them. Plain, confident tone; no jargon, no exclamation-stacking, no manufactured urgency.

QUALITY BAR: every screen should leave the user feeling capable and one small, obvious step from value — not overwhelmed by choice.
</instructions>
